1.title: Molar mass of carbon dioxide by gas weighing
1.focus: Determine a gas molar mass from a corrected mass difference and pV = nRT.
1.equipment: 100 mL gas-tight syringe with cap; 0.001 g balance; thermometer; barometer; prepared bag of dry CO2 and dry air; gas tubing.
1.safety: Teacher handles gas supply; use small ambient-pressure gas bags in a ventilated room. No heating, needles or rigidly restrained heated syringe. Keep the same dry syringe, cap and external volume for every weighing.
method: Check that the syringe moves freely and is leak-tight. Flush with dry air, draw exactly 100.0 mL at room pressure, cap and weigh the complete assembly.
Record room temperature and atmospheric pressure. Uncap before changing volume.
Flush the syringe three times with CO2 from the prepared bag. Let the freely moving plunger settle at atmospheric pressure, then adjust to 100.0 mL, cap and weigh promptly.
Repeat the air and CO2 measurements twice. Keep temperature, volume and all fittings identical. Record any volume drift; reject a leaking run.
Calculate Δm = mass with CO2 − mass with air. Calculate n = pV/RT using Pa, m³ and K. Then M(CO2) = 28.97 + Δm/n in g mol−1. The air correction is essential.
1.results: Run; air mass / g; CO2 mass / g; Δm / g; V / mL; T / K; p / Pa; M / g mol−1.
questions: Why is Δm not the CO2 mass?
How does an air leak affect the inferred value?

1.change: Replaces heated hexane with room-temperature gas weighing. Removes the fixed-plunger contradiction and adds an explicit air-mass correction.
1.skills: Gas mass difference; pV = nRT; repeated readings; uncertainty and air correction.
1.prep: Prepare dry gas in ambient-pressure bags using the department gas-supply procedure. This air-reference adaptation uses equal external volume to cancel buoyancy differences. Trial three pairs: expect a positive mass difference near 0.06 g for 100 mL at room conditions. Record measured spread; do not claim an exact value of 44.01.
answers: Why is Δm not the CO2 mass?
The starting syringe already contains air. Δm is the mass of CO2 minus the mass of the same amount of air.
How does an air leak affect the inferred value?
It reduces the CO2–air mass difference and biases the molar mass towards that of air.
What makes this measurement demanding?
A roughly 0.06 g mass difference requires a 0.001 g balance, stable temperature and leak-free, dry gas handling.

2.title: Water of crystallisation in magnesium sulfate
2.time: 60 min plus any further cooling cycles
2.focus: Determine water of crystallisation by gravimetry; distinguish constant mass from one timed heating.
2.equipment: About 2 g labelled MgSO4·7H2O; crucible and lid; balance preferably 0.001 g; burner, pipe-clay triangle, tripod, tongs and heatproof mat.
2.safety: Wear splash goggles. Handle hot equipment with tongs; cool to room temperature before weighing. Heat gently first to prevent spitting; do not leave a flame unattended.
method: Weigh the clean, dry crucible and lid. Add about 2 g hydrate and reweigh.
With the lid slightly ajar, warm gently until visible water evolution subsides; then heat more strongly for the technician-trialled period.
Replace the lid, cool fully in the agreed dry location and weigh.
Repeat heating for two minutes, cooling fully and weighing until successive masses agree within the declared balance tolerance. Record every mass.
Calculate hydrate mass, residue mass and water lost. Use n(H2O) = water mass/18.02 and n(MgSO4) = residue mass/120.37.
Report x in MgSO4·xH2O with an uncertainty discussion. Do not force an unexpected result to 7.
2.results: Crucible + lid / g; initial total / g; each cooled total / g; mass change between cycles / g.
questions: Does constant mass prove anhydrous salt?

2.change: Adds a defined constant-mass criterion, hydration check and trial of complete dehydration.
2.skills: Heat, cool and reweigh to constant mass; mole ratios; direction of error.
2.prep: Verify the bottle is heptahydrate. Pilot the actual crucible, flame and cooling routine against x ≈ 7 before issue. Set constant-mass tolerance from the balance, e.g. 0.002 g on a suitable 0.001 g balance; never promise that a fixed number of heating cycles is sufficient.
answers: Why cool before weighing?
Hot objects create unstable balance readings and can damage the balance.
Effect of incomplete dehydration?
Water loss is too small and residue too large, so calculated x is too low.
Does constant mass prove anhydrous salt?
No. A stable partially dehydrated residue is possible; the known hydrate and heating routine need a pilot.

3.title: Empirical formula of magnesium oxide
3.focus: Determine an empirical formula from a mass gain and evaluate whether the gain is large enough to measure.
3.equipment: Clean Mg ribbon giving about 0.20 g; crucible/lid; 0.001 g balance; emery paper; tongs; tripod/triangle; burner and mat.
3.safety: Wear goggles. Do not look directly at burning magnesium. Keep the lid over the crucible, lifting briefly for oxygen; retain the smoke. Cool before weighing.
method: Clean ribbon to remove surface oxide. Weigh dry crucible and lid, then add about 0.20 g coiled ribbon and record the total.
Heat gently then strongly with the lid on; briefly lift it at intervals to admit air while minimising loss of white oxide.
Continue until no shiny magnesium is visible. Cool fully with the lid on and weigh.
Reheat, cool and reweigh to constant mass within the specified balance tolerance.
Calculate Mg mass and mass gained as oxygen. Divide by 24.31 and 16.00 respectively and determine the simplest mole ratio.
Compare with 1:1 and discuss smoke loss, incomplete oxidation and possible nitride formation.
3.results: Crucible + lid / g; initial total / g; cooled product totals / g; Mg mass / g; oxygen gain / g.
questions: Why lift and replace the lid?

3.change: Replaces an arbitrary ribbon length with a measurable mass and protects oxygen-gain precision.
3.skills: Crucible and lid technique; constant mass; mass gain; empirical formula.
3.prep: Trial the approximate 0.20 g loading with the crucible capacity and ventilation. Expected oxygen gain is about 0.13 g if conversion is complete. Do not add water to a hot residue. Set constant-mass tolerance and include cooling time.
answers: Why clean the ribbon?
Surface oxide would be counted as starting magnesium and distort the mass-gain calculation.
Why lift and replace the lid?
Oxygen is needed, but the lid limits loss of product smoke.
Effect of losing oxide?
Measured oxygen gain is too small; the calculated Mg:O ratio is too high.

4.title: Molar mass of a diprotic acid by titration
4.lesson: Year 12 · 12 RP01 Practical: Carrying Out Titration; 13 RP01 Analysis: Titration Calculations
4.focus: Combine volumetric solution preparation, diprotic stoichiometry and titration to determine Mr.
4.equipment: 1.8–2.2 g succinic acid labelled unknown diprotic acid; balance; 250.0 mL flask; 25.0 mL pipette; burette; standardised 0.1000 M NaOH; phenolphthalein.
4.safety: Wear goggles; avoid acid/alkali contact. Use a pipette filler. Fill the burette below eye level. Wash splashes promptly as instructed.
method: Record the exact mass of the acid. Dissolve it in deionised water, transfer quantitatively into a 250.0 mL volumetric flask, make to the mark at room temperature and invert repeatedly.
Rinse/fill the burette with the acid solution and remove the funnel. Pipette 25.0 mL of standardised NaOH into a conical flask.
Add two drops of phenolphthalein. Titrate acid into the swirling alkali until the last faint pink disappears.
Take a rough titre, then repeat with fresh aliquots until at least two accurate titres agree within 0.10 mL. Record all readings to the burette precision.
Use n(acid aliquot) = n(NaOH)/2. Find acid concentration, total acid moles in 250.0 mL and Mr = mass/moles.
4.results: Run; initial and final burette / mL; titre / mL; included in mean?; exact solid mass / g; labelled NaOH concentration.
questions: Why divide NaOH moles by two?
Expected titre for 2.000 g and exactly 0.1000 M NaOH?
Why is rinsing the burette with water alone unsuitable?
4.student_src: Source copies/01 - Year 12 (AS) Lessons/01 - Atomic Structure and Moles/_Shared Resources/1.5 - The Mole/Kerboodle/2.4 - Practical MR - IMPROVED v1.0.docx
4.change: Clarifies acid identity, diprotic ratio, endpoint direction and concordance.
4.skills: Make a solution from a weighed solid; concordant titres; stoichiometry; Mr.
answers: Why divide NaOH moles by two?
Succinic acid is diprotic and reacts with two moles of hydroxide per mole.
Expected titre for 2.000 g and exactly 0.1000 M NaOH?
About 18.45 mL, using Mr 118.09.
Why is rinsing the burette with water alone unsuitable?
Residual water dilutes the acid, increasing the titre and biasing the result.
4.prep: Use standardised NaOH and disclose its measured concentration. Supply enough acid for three accurate titres plus a rough run. Pilot endpoint and confirm the expected 17–21 mL range.

5.title: Precision and accuracy in acid base titration
5.lesson: Year 12 · 11 RP01 Planning: Titration Method; 12 RP01 Practical: Carrying Out Titration
5.focus: Develop repeatable endpoint judgement and separate precision from accuracy.
5.equipment: 0.07350 M potassium hydrogenphthalate (KHP); approximately 0.1000 M standardised NaOH; 25.0 mL pipette; burette; conical flasks; phenolphthalein.
5.safety: Wear goggles; use a filler and rinse apparatus with its own solution. Avoid touching the burette tip to the receiving solution.
method: Record the stated KHP concentration. Rinse and fill the burette with KHP solution.
Pipette 25.0 mL NaOH into a flask and add two drops of phenolphthalein.
Add KHP while swirling until the final faint pink disappears. Take one rough titre.
Repeat using fresh NaOH until at least two accurate titres agree within 0.10 mL. Keep all readings; explain exclusions.
Use the 1:1 KHP:NaOH ratio to calculate NaOH concentration. Compare individual concordance with the class spread.
Only after calculation, obtain the reference NaOH concentration and calculate percentage difference. Discuss whether averaging could remove a systematic error.
5.results: Rough and repeat burette readings / mL; mean titre / mL; calculated and reference concentration / mol dm−3.
questions: Why is the class mean not proof of accuracy?

5.change: Adds individual concordant repeats and a reference for accuracy.
5.skills: Pipette and burette use; rough versus accurate titres; class data; precision.
answers: What demonstrates precision?
Close agreement between independent repeated titres.
Why is the class mean not proof of accuracy?
Every group may share a biased reagent concentration or endpoint convention.
Expected titre?
34.01 mL for 25.0 mL of exactly 0.1000 M NaOH and 0.07350 M KHP.

6.title: Ethanoic acid concentration in vinegar
6.lesson: Year 12 · 12 RP01 Practical: Carrying Out Titration; 13 RP01 Analysis: Titration Calculations
6.focus: Track a dilution factor through an authentic acid–base assay.
6.equipment: Clear vinegar; 25.0 mL pipette; 250.0 mL volumetric flask; burette; standardised 0.1000 M NaOH; phenolphthalein.
6.safety: Wear goggles; use a filler. Do not taste the vinegar. Use clean, correctly rinsed volumetric equipment.
method: Pipette 25.0 mL vinegar into a 250.0 mL volumetric flask. Add water to the mark and invert to mix.
Rinse/fill the burette with diluted vinegar. Pipette 25.0 mL NaOH into a flask and add two drops phenolphthalein.
Titrate until the last faint pink disappears. Take a rough run then at least two accurate titres within 0.10 mL.
Calculate acid concentration using the 1:1 reaction. Multiply by ten for the original vinegar.
Convert to g ethanoic acid per 100 mL using Mr 60.05. Compare cautiously with the product label.
6.results: Burette readings/titres / mL; NaOH concentration; dilution factor; original acid concentration and g per 100 mL.
questions: What does a 30.00 mL mean titre imply?

method: Record the exact CaCO3 mass in a beaker. Add 50.00 mL standard HCl gradually; cover loosely with a watch glass during reaction.

Calculate recovered CaCO3 mass and percentage recovery against the weighed sample.

17.title: Quantitative calorimetry instead of alcohol combustion
17.lesson: Year 12 · 25 RP02 Practical: Measuring Enthalpy Change; 26 RP02 Analysis: Hess's Law Context
17.focus: Measure a quantitative enthalpy change with an explicit heat-loss evaluation.
17.equipment: 25.0 mL 1.00 M HCl and 25.0 mL 1.00 M NaOH per run; insulated cup in beaker with loose lid; temperature probe 0.1°C; cylinders; timer; stirrer; balance.
17.safety: Wear goggles; avoid acid/alkali contact. Support the cup in a beaker. Do not seal the vessel. Rinse splashes promptly; retain solutions for instructed disposal.
method: Bring the two solutions to the same room temperature. Record actual concentrations and the empty cup mass.
Place 25.0 mL HCl in the insulated cup. Record temperature every 30 seconds for three minutes; measure the NaOH temperature separately.
At exactly three minutes add 25.0 mL NaOH, replace the loose lid, stir gently and continue readings every 30 seconds for five minutes.
Weigh the cup plus mixture after temperature recording to estimate actual solution mass, keeping the cup dry externally.
Plot temperature against time and extrapolate the post-reaction cooling trend back to mixing time. Use the corresponding baseline temperature to estimate corrected ΔT.
Calculate q = m × 4.18 × ΔT in joules and ΔH = −q/n, with n the moles of water formed. Repeat and compare.
17.results: Time / s; temperature / °C; mixing time; solution mass / g; reagent volumes/concentrations; corrected ΔT; ΔH / kJ mol−1.
questions: Why include both solutions in m?
What does the correction not remove?
17.student_src: Source copies/01 - Year 12 (AS) Lessons/04 - Energetics/_Shared Resources/4.1 - Enthalpy Change (3.1.4.1)/Kerboodle/4.3 - Practical - IMPROVED v1.0.docx
17.change: Replaces alcohol-burning calorimetry with the adopted quantitative neutralisation method. Fuel combustion is retained only as a written evaluation comparison.
17.skills: Temperature logging; controlled volumes; heat-loss extrapolation; q = mcΔT; molar enthalpy.
answers: Expected sign and approximate scale?
Exothermic; a few degrees rise, with ideal strong-acid/strong-base ΔH near −57 kJ mol−1. Simple apparatus usually underestimates its magnitude.
Why include both solutions in m?
Both receive the released energy; using only one volume halves the estimated heat.
What does the correction not remove?
Heat absorbed by apparatus, imperfect insulation/mixing and assumptions about density and specific heat remain.
17.prep: For three runs per pair allow at least 90 mL of each solution. Verify probe response, equal initial temperatures and an observable approximately 6–7°C rise. Do not seal the lid around the probe. Model the extrapolation before expecting independent interpretation.

24.title: Equilibrium constant from a prepared ester mixture
24.lesson: Year 12 · 46 Equilibrium Constant Kc; 47 Kc Calculations
24.mode: Student titration of technician-prepared equilibrium mixture
24.time: 50–60 min plus analysis; preparation at least one week earlier
24.focus: Determine equilibrium amounts by titration, including subtraction of acid catalyst.
24.equipment: Prepared mixture of ethanol/ethanoic acid/HCl catalyst; preparation record; accurate 3.00 mL graduated pipette; 0.5000 M NaOH; burette; phenolphthalein; water.
24.safety: Wear goggles. Mixture is flammable and acidic; no flames. Do not smell or heat. Keep stock sealed between sampling. Only the technician prepares/stores the equilibrium batch.
method: Read the batch record: actual initial amounts of ethanol, ethanoic acid, water and HCl, mixing date, storage temperature and total sampled mixture volume.
Mix the stock consistently. Transfer an accurate 3.00 mL aliquot into 20 mL water.
Titrate promptly with standard NaOH to a faint pink endpoint persisting for 10 seconds. Do not keep adding alkali to chase long-term fading.
Repeat with fresh aliquots until accurate titres agree within 0.10 mL.
Subtract HCl catalyst moles in the aliquot from total titratable acid. Convert the remaining ethanoic acid to the amount in the original mixture.
Use initial/change/equilibrium amounts to calculate ester and water formed. Calculate Kc = [ester][water]/([acid][ethanol]) and discuss approximations.

Record actual masses, purity and water content from stock data; do not assume 5 mL HCl solution is 5 g water. Leave at least a week. Pilot replicate aliquots and confirm stable titres over an additional interval before issuing. Use standardised 0.5000 M NaOH: a 3.00 mL aliquot of this batch should give a titre around 20–25 mL, subject to actual composition and equilibrium. The weaker 0.1000 M titrant would require roughly 100 mL and is unsuitable for one burette fill.

It consumes alkali but is not ethanoic acid in the equilibrium expression.
Why can a delayed endpoint drift?
Alkaline hydrolysis of ester can consume further hydroxide.
Why is the result approximate?
Composition/water estimates, sampling, equilibrium attainment and endpoint chemistry limit accuracy.

38.change: Measures actual volume, uses stable pH readings and prioritises the two RP9 pairings.

answers: Expected equivalence volumes?
About 25.0 mL for both nominally equal concentrations.
Why are equivalence pH values different?
Ethanoate hydrolyses to give an alkaline equivalence mixture; ammonium gives an acidic one.
Does adding immersion water change equivalence volume?
It changes concentrations/pH but not the original analyte moles, so not the stoichiometric equivalence volume.

39.title: Acid strength using a conductivity probe
39.lesson: Year 13 · 29 Weak Acids and Ka; 27 pH of Strong Acids
39.time: 25 min student work or 10–15 min demo
39.focus: Distinguish acid strength from concentration using controlled conductivity comparisons.
39.equipment: Conductivity probe/meter with calibration standard; water blank; 0.100 M HCl and ethanoic acid; beakers; thermometer; optional coded sample from the same two stocks.
39.safety: Wear goggles; use the sensor according to its range/immersion instructions. No 8 V DC electrolysis circuit. Rinse the probe between samples.
method: Calibrate/check the conductivity meter using its specified standard. Record temperature.
Measure the water blank and then 25 mL portions of each equal-concentration acid, keeping probe immersion and temperature constant.
Wait for stable readings, record units and repeat after rinsing.
If given a coded sample known to be one of these two stocks, classify it by comparison; state that this restricted choice is essential.
Explain the conductivity difference using degree of ionisation and mobile ions.
Predict why a more concentrated weak acid cannot be classified simply by comparing it with an arbitrary dilute strong acid.
39.results: Sample; stated concentration; temperature; conductivity and units; repeat; inference.
questions: Why does HCl usually conduct more here?
Is concentration the same as strength?
Can conductivity uniquely identify an arbitrary acid?

39.change: Replaces the DC circuit with a proper conductivity sensor and constrains the unknown inference.
39.skills: Control concentration/electrode geometry; compare conductivity; explain ionisation.
39.prep: Check the meter range for 0.100 M HCl and use a suitable calibration standard. Supply equal-temperature stocks. Only use an unknown selected from the stated matched pair. Collect solutions as directed by local guidance.
answers: Why does HCl usually conduct more here?
At equal concentration it is much more extensively ionised, producing more mobile ions.
Is concentration the same as strength?
No. Concentration is amount per volume; strength describes extent of ionisation.
Can conductivity uniquely identify an arbitrary acid?
No. Concentration, ion mobility, temperature and other dissolved ions all matter.

answers: First protonation equation?
CO3²− + H+ → HCO3−.
Second stage?
HCO3− + H+ → CO2 + H2O.

Two moles of H+ are required per initial mole of carbonate for complete neutralisation.

43.title: Chirality and optical rotation
43.lesson: Year 13 · 50 Chirality and Enantiomers; 51 Racemic Mixtures and Applications
43.focus: Demonstrate non-superimposable mirror images and interpret optical rotation.
43.change: Adopts models and optical-rotation data, making subjective smell optional.
43.skills: Interpret evidence; distinguish observations from model data; justify a chemical conclusion.
answers: What makes the centre stereogenic?
Four different substituent paths/groups around the tetrahedral carbon.
Why is the equal mixture optically inactive?
Equal and opposite rotations cancel under the same conditions.
Does zero rotation prove no chiral molecules?
No. A racemate contains chiral molecules; cancellation or other limitations can give zero net rotation.
questions: Why is the equal mixture optically inactive?
Does zero rotation prove no chiral molecules?

44.title: Small scale preparation of an ester
44.lesson: Year 13 · 57 Esters: Formation, Hydrolysis and Uses

answers: Product and equation?
Pentyl ethanoate: CH3COOH + HO(CH2)4CH3 ⇌ CH3COO(CH2)4CH3 + H2O.
Role of sulfuric acid?
Acid catalyst; it speeds approach to equilibrium.
Why carbonate?
It neutralises residual acids, releasing CO2; gradual addition prevents overflow.

45.title: Aspirin synthesis purification and melting range

answers: Theoretical mass from 6.00 g salicylic acid?
6.00 × 180.16/138.12 ≈ 7.83 g aspirin, with anhydride in excess.
Why can purification reduce yield but improve quality?
Impurities are removed, but some aspirin remains dissolved or is lost during transfers.
What would a broad depressed melting range suggest?
Impurity, residual solvent or decomposition; it is evidence to investigate, not a definitive purity percentage.

What would a broad depressed melting range suggest?

answers: Why test aldehyde separately from alcohol oxidation?
Both an aldehyde and a primary alcohol can reduce acidified dichromate; Fehling distinguishes the aldehyde within this set.
Does ordinary phenol give the carboxylic-acid carbonate fizz test?
No. Salicylic acid does so because it contains COOH as well as phenol.
How are all five assigned?

Acid: carbonate fizz; aldehyde: Fehling positive; alcohol: oxidation positive/Fehling negative; alkene: bromine positive with aldehyde excluded; ketone: remaining negative pattern within the declared set.

47.title: Unsaturation testing with prepared bromine water
47.lesson: Year 12 · 72 Electrophilic Addition Reactions; 84 RP06 Practical: Carry Out Tests
47.focus: Use controls to infer unsaturation without claiming unique identity.
47.equipment: Cyclohexane, cyclohexene and limonene in labelled dropping bottles; fresh 0.02 M bromine water; small glass tubes; pipettes; white background.
47.safety: Wear goggles; use a ventilated laboratory and the department bromine procedure. No flames or direct smelling. Collect organic/bromine waste as directed; use glass or a verified solvent-compatible plate.
method: Label three clean tubes with the known compounds and a fourth as reagent blank.
Add 0.5 mL bromine water to each. Add two drops of the appropriate organic liquid to each test tube; leave the blank without organic liquid.
Mix carefully using the teacher-demonstrated technique and compare both phases after the same interval.
Record whether colour persists anywhere in the mixture; transfer of bromine into an organic layer is not decolourisation.
Use cyclohexane as a negative and cyclohexene as a positive control. Explain the limonene result.
For a coded sample, conclude whether the test supports C=C under these conditions; do not claim unique molecular identity.
